title: Canadian Citizenship Act 1946 comes into effect. Among other things this changed federal law such that Canadian women no longer lost their citizenship automatically if they married non-Canadians.
text: The Canadian Citizenship Act was a statute passed by the Parliament of Canada in 1946 which created the legal status of Canadian citizenship. The Act defined who were Canadian citizens, separate and independent from the status of the British subject and repealed earlier Canadian legislation relating to Canadian nationals and citizens as sub-classes of British subject status.

title: Dominion of Newfoundland (later a province in 1949) switches to driving on the right from the left.
text: The Dominion of Newfoundland, or simply Newfoundland, was a British Dominion in eastern North America, today the modern Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador. It included the island of Newfoundland, and Labrador on the continental mainland.

title: The cabinet order deporting Japanese-Canadians to Japan is repealed after widespread protests.
text: Japanese Canadians are Canadian citizens of Japanese ancestry. Japanese Canadians are mostly concentrated in Western Canada, especially in the province of British Columbia, which hosts the largest Japanese community in the country with the majority of them living in and around Vancouver.

title: The oil well Leduc No. 1 comes in, launching the Alberta oil industry.
text: Leduc No. 1 was a major crude oil discovery made near Leduc, Alberta, Canada, on February 13, 1947.

title: The Chinese Immigration Act of 1923 is repealed.
text: The Chinese Immigration Act, 1923, also known as the "Chinese Exclusion Act" (the duration of which has been dubbed the Exclusion Era), was a Canadian Act of Parliament passed by the government of Liberal Prime Minister William Lyon Mackenzie King, banning most forms of Chinese immigration to Canada. Immigration from most countries was controlled or restricted in some way, but only the Chinese were completely proh…

title: Two new nuclear reactors go online at the Chalk River research facility.
text: Chalk River Laboratories is a Canadian nuclear research facility in Deep River, about 180 km (110 mi) north-west of Ottawa. CRL is a site of significant research and development to support and advance nuclear technology, particularly CANDU reactor technology.

title: Two Canadian National Railways (CNR) passenger trains collide head-on at Dugald, Manitoba, resulting in 31 people dead and 85 people injured. The disaster is exacerbated by the CNR's use of wooden passenger coaches, as strict rationing of…
text: The Canadian National Railway Company (reporting mark CN) is a Canadian Class I freight railway headquartered in Montreal, Quebec, which serves Canada and the Midwestern and Southern United States. It is one of Canada's two main freight rail companies, along with Canadian Pacific Kansas City.

title: The last group of personnel who had been on active service, for World War II, since September 1, 1939, stood down.
text: World War II, or the Second World War, was a global conflict between two coalitions: the Allies and the Axis powers. Nearly all of the world's countries participated, with many engaging in total war on an unprecedented scale.

title: New letters patent defining the office and powers of the governor general come into effect.
text: The Letters Patent, 1947, are letters patent signed by George VI, as King of Canada, on 8 September 1947 and came into effect on 1 October of the same year. These letters, replacing the previous letters patent issued in 1931, reconstituted the Office of the governor general of Canada under the terms of the Constitution Act, 1867, expanding the governor general's ability to exercise the royal prerogative, thereby a…

title: Boss Johnson becomes premier of British Columbia.
text: Byron Ingemar "Boss" Johnson, served as the 24th premier of British Columbia, from 1947 to 1952. To his contemporaries he was often referred to by his nickname, Boss Johnson, which had nothing to do with his personality, but was an anglicization of the Icelandic "Bjossi", which is a diminutive form of his birth-name of Bjorn, which was adapted into English as Byron.

title: Stephen Leacock Award: Harry L. Symons, Ojibway Melody.
text: The Stephen Leacock Memorial Medal for Humour, also known as the Stephen Leacock Medal for Humour or just the Leacock Medal, is an annual Canadian literary award presented for the best book of humour written in English by a Canadian writer, published or self-published in the previous year. The silver medal, designed by sculptor Emanuel Hahn, is a tribute to well-known Canadian humorist Stephen Leacock and is accom…
wiki: Stephen Leacock Memorial Medal for Humour

title: Fearful Symmetry - Northrop Frye
text: Herman Northrop Frye was a Canadian literary critic and literary theorist, considered one of the most influential of the 20th century. Frye gained international fame with his first book, Fearful Symmetry (1947), which led to the reinterpretation of the poetry of William Blake.

title: Who Has Seen the Wind? - W.O. Mitchell
text: William Ormond Mitchell was a Canadian writer and broadcaster. His "best-loved" novel is Who Has Seen the Wind (1947), which portrays life on the Canadian Prairies from the point of view of a small boy and sold almost a million copies in Canada.

title: The Toronto Maple Leafs win their sixth Stanley Cup by defeating the Montreal Canadiens 4 games to 2. The deciding Game 6 was played in Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto.
text: The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff champion. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America, and the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) considers it to be one of the "most important championships available to the sport".

title: The Ontario Hockey Association's Toronto St. Michael's Majors win their third (and last until 1961) Memorial Cup by defeating Southern Saskatchewan Junior Hockey League's Moose Jaw Canucks 4 games to 3. The deciding Game 7 was played at…
text: The Ontario Hockey League) is one of the three major junior ice hockey leagues which constitute the Canadian Hockey League, alongside the Western Hockey League and the Quebec Maritimes Junior Hockey League. The league is for players aged 16–20.

title: The Toronto Argonauts win their eighth Grey Cup by defeating the Winnipeg Blue Bombers 10 to 9 in the 35th Grey Cup played in Varsity Stadium in Toronto. This was the last Grey Cup to be won by a team with all Canadian players.
text: The Grey Cup is both the championship game of the Canadian Football League (CFL) and the trophy awarded to the victorious team playing in the namesake championship of professional Canadian football. The game is contested between the winners of the CFL's East and West divisional playoffs and is one of Canadian television's largest annual sporting events.

title: “Near You” by Francis Craig
text: "Near You" is a popular song written and originally recorded by Francis Craig and His Orchestra at Castle Studio in 1947, with lyrics by Kermit Goell, which became a pop standard.

title: “Peg o' My Heart” by The Harmonicats
text: "Peg o' My Heart" is a popular song with lyrics by Alfred Bryan and music by Fred Fisher. It was published on March 15, 1913 and it featured in the 1913 musical Ziegfeld Follies.
listen: Peg o' My Heart The Harmonicats

title: “Heartaches” by Ted Weems
text: "Heartaches" is a song written by composer Al Hoffman and lyricist John Klenner and originally published in 1931. A fast-tempo instrumental version of the song by Ted Weems and his Orchestra became a major hit in 1947, topping the Billboard Best Selling Singles chart in the US. Later versions by band leader Harry James and doo-wop group the Marcels were also chart hits.

title: “Linda” by Ray Noble Orchestra and Buddy Clark
text: "Linda" is a popular song written and published in 1946 by Jack Lawrence. The song is notable for being named after then-one-year-old Linda McCartney.
listen: Linda Ray Noble Orchestra and Buddy Clark

title: “I Wish I Didn't Love You So” by Vaughn Monroe
text: "I Wish I Didn't Love You So" is a 1947 song written by Frank Loesser. It was originally performed by Betty Hutton for the 1947 Paramount Pictures film The Perils of Pauline, and was made famous by Vaughn Monroe and His Orchestra, who reached number 2 with the song in the United States, and number 1 in Canada.
wiki: I Wish I Didn't Love You So
listen: I Wish I Didn't Love You So Vaughn Monroe

title: “The Anniversary Song” by Al Jolson
text: "Waves of the Danube" is a waltz composed by Ion Ivanovici in 1880, and is one of the most famous Romanian tunes in the world. The song has many variations throughout the piece, reminiscent of the music of Johann Strauss.

title: “That's My Desire” by Sammy Kaye
text: "That's My Desire" is a 1931 popular song with music by Helmy Kresa and lyrics by Carroll Loveday. The highest-charting version of the song was recorded by the Sammy Kaye orchestra in 1946, although a version of the song recorded by Frankie Laine has become better known over the years, being one of Laine's best-known recordings.

title: “Ballerina” by Vaughn Monroe
text: "Ballerina" is a popular song, sometimes known as "Dance, Ballerina, Dance". The song was written by Carl Sigman with lyrics by Sidney Keith 'Bob' Russell.
wiki: Ballerina (Sidney Keith Russell and Carl Sigman song)

title: “Managua, Nicaragua” by Freddy Martin
text: "Managua, Nicaragua" is a popular American song from 1946, whose music was written by Irving Fields, and lyrics by Albert Gamse.

title: “Mam'selle” by Art Lund
text: "Mam'selle" is a bittersweet song about a rendez-vous with a "mam'selle" in a small café. The music was written by Edmund Goulding, the lyrics by Mack Gordon.

title: “Chi-Baba, Chi-Baba (My Bambino Go to Sleep)” by Perry Como
text: "Chi-Baba, Chi-Baba" is a popular song written by Mack David, Jerry Livingston, and Al Hoffman, and published in 1947.

title: “Temptation (Tim-Tayshun)” by Red Ingle and The Natural Seven and Jo Stafford
text: "Temptation" is a popular song published in 1933, with music written by Nacio Herb Brown and lyrics by Arthur Freed.

title: “I Wonder Who's Kissing Her Now” by Ted Weems and Perry Como
text: "I Wonder Who's Kissing Her Now" is a popular song. The music was written by Harold Orlob, the lyrics by Will M. Hough and Frank R. Adams.
wiki: I Wonder Who's Kissing Her Now
listen: I Wonder Who's Kissing Her Now Ted Weems and Perry Como

title: “The Old Lamp-Lighter” by Sammy Kaye
text: "The Old Lamp-Lighter" is a popular song. The music was written by Nat Simon, the lyrics by Charles Tobias.

title: “When You Were Sweet Sixteen” by Perry Como
text: "When You Were Sweet Sixteen" is popular song written by James Thornton and published in 1898. Inspired and sung by the composer's wife, the ballad quickly became a hit song in vaudeville.
listen: When You Were Sweet Sixteen Perry Como

title: “How Soon” by Jack Owens and Eddie Ballantine
text: "How Soon" is a 1947 song written by Jack Owens and Carroll Lucas, performed by Owens and backed by Eddie Ballantine's orchestra. It was originally made popular by Owens, and later Vaughn Monroe in the same year.
wiki: How Soon (Will I Be Seeing You?)
listen: How Soon Jack Owens and Eddie Ballantine

text: "Too Fat Polka" is a novelty song by Ross MacLean and Arthur Richardson. The song is known for its recurrent chorus, "I don't want her, you can have her, she's too fat for me." A 1947 recording by Arthur Godfrey, with orchestra under the direction of Archie Bleyer, reached No.

title: “I Wonder, I Wonder, I Wonder” by Eddy Howard
text: Edward Evan Duncan Howard was an American vocalist and bandleader who was popular during the 1940s and 1950s,
listen: I Wonder, I Wonder, I Wonder Eddy Howard

title: “My Adobe Hacienda” by Eddy Howard
text: "My Adobe Hacienda" is a song composed by Louise Massey and Lee Penny. It first became popular in 1941 with Massey's recorded version, where it placed at #23.

title: “Huggin' and Chalkin'” by Hoagy Carmichael
text: Hoagland Howard Carmichael was an American musician, composer, songwriter, actor, author and lawyer. Carmichael was one of the most successful Tin Pan Alley songwriters of the 1930s and 1940s, and was among the first singer-songwriters in the age of mass media to use new communication technologies such as radio broadcasts, television, microphones, and sound recordings (musical records).

title: “(I Love You) For Sentimental Reasons” by King Cole Trio
text: " for Sentimental Reasons" is a popular song written by Ivory "Deek" Watson, founding member of the Ink Spots and of the Brown Dots, and William "Pat" Best, founding member of the Four Tunes. The credits and Duchess Music list Watson as a co-writer.
listen: (I Love You) For Sentimental Reasons King Cole Trio

title: “Ole Buttermilk Sky” by Hoagy Carmichael
text: "Ole Buttermilk Sky" is a song written by Hoagy Carmichael which was first a hit in 1946 for big band leader and old-time radio personality Kay Kyser. It has been covered by a multitude of artists / singers over the years and decades since.

title: “You Do” by Vaughn Monroe
text: Vaughn Wilton Monroe was an American baritone singer, trumpeter and big band leader who was most popular in the 1940s and 1950s. He has two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, one for recording and another for radio performance.

title: “White Christmas” by Bing Crosby
text: "White Christmas" is a song reminiscing about an old-fashioned Christmas setting. Written by Irving Berlin for the 1942 musical film Holiday Inn, the song won the Academy Award for Best Original Song at the 15th Academy Awards.

title: “Across the Alley from the Alamo” by The Mills Brothers
text: "Across the Alley from the Alamo" is a song written in 1946 by Joe Greene, which has become a jazz standard. Greene's whimsical lyrics, concern a Navajo Indian and his pinto pony.
wiki: Across the Alley from the Alamo
listen: Across the Alley from the Alamo The Mills Brothers

title: “Civilization” by Danny Kaye and The Andrews Sisters with Vic Schoen
text: "Civilization" is an American traditional pop song. It was written by Bob Hilliard and Carl Sigman, published in 1947 and later included in the 1947 Broadway musical Angel in the Wings, sung by Elaine Stritch.
wiki: Civilization (Bob Hilliard and Carl Sigman song)
listen: Civilization Danny Kaye and The Andrews Sisters with Vic Schoen

title: “Open the Door, Richard!” by Count Basie
text: "Open the Door, Richard" is a song first recorded by the saxophonist Jack McVea in 1946 for Black & White Records at the suggestion of A&R man Ralph Bass. In 1947, it was the number one song on Billboard's "Honor Roll of Hits".
listen: Open the Door, Richard! Count Basie

title: “Feudin' and Fightin'” by Dorothy Shay
text: "Feudin' and Fightin'" is a song written by Al Dubin and Burton Lane, sung by Dorothy Shay, and released in 1947 on the Columbia label (catalog no. 37189).

title: “The Whiffenpoof Song” by Bing Crosby with Fred Waring
text: The Yale Whiffenpoofs is a collegiate a cappella singing group at Yale University. Established in 1909, it is the oldest such group in the United States.
